title: The Radium Girls...of Social Media
subtitle: A Conversation with Carlene MacMillan, MD, FCTMSS, DFAACAP
body_html:
Today’s column is a conversation about the role of product decisions on the mental health of youth, as understood by my wife, .

Advertising Moment: Inessential Pharmacology

I have a new IN-PRINT book available for purchase. Inessential Pharmacology is available from Amazon (affiliate link), in both hardback and paperback. A Kindle ebook and an unsettling AI audio version are also available.

Introduce yourself to our audience.

I am Carlene MacMillan, a psychiatrist by training, still practicing a little bit. I’m the Chief Product Officer at Radial and the co-chair of the Public Resource Committee at the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. And a mom to twin almost-10-year-olds, next week.

You’ve been getting asked to speak about the recent Meta lawsuit verdicts. What’s your take?

Yes, the verdicts that came down in California and New Mexico. I’m getting asked about them because I’m probably the only child psychiatrist who’s also in product and does work with AACAP around how to communicate with the public about social media and technology. So my perspective is unique.

I’ve gotten sick of the only comparisons being to tobacco. I feel like there’s a more apt comparison for how this might play out, and that’s the Radium Girls from the 1920s and 1930s.

Tell us about the Radium Girls.

So radium, it glows in the dark, looks really cool. They didn’t really understand then that it was bad. Keep in mind this is the Marie Curie era, like radium, radiology, it’s been a super important element to the rest of history. But at the time, people just thought it was a cool thing that glowed in the dark that could illuminate watch dials. So all these factories came up where they would hire young women, some of them teenagers, to do the painting. The technique required taking the paintbrush between the lips to create a fine point, dipping it in the radium paint, painting the dial, and repeating. They were constantly getting radium in their mouths. But that was fine, because at the time, people thought it was this miracle thing that was good for health.

For our readers, radium is a naturally occurring element, highly radioactive, silvery white, with an atomic number of 88. It glows in the dark naturally.

Yes, it glows in the dark, that’s the key thing. It’s like magical. And there were celebrities endorsing it, using it every day, sort of like some of the influencers today pushing the latest wellness trends. Radium was the best thing ever. Being a Radium Girl was actually a prestigious job for these young women, who had very few other opportunities. They even wore the paint on their dresses and skin for parties, glowing magically in the dark. It really paints a beautiful picture; there’s actually a play and podcast about it for exactly that reason.

Then, things went horrifically wrong.

The chemical process, as I understand it from teaching MCAT chemistry, is that radium biologically mimics calcium. It’s a Group 2 alkaline earth metal, right next to calcium on the periodic table, so the body just incorporates radium wherever calcium would go. When you put it in your mouth, it gets built right into your bones and teeth.

Yes, and so over time these women started to fall ill. Mysterious tooth problems, back problems, unexplained deterioration. What was happening, and what the factory managers came to know, was that it starts getting incorporated into the teeth and jaw, and just begins eating everything alive from the inside. Rotting it away. It’s really scary looking. If you watch Fallout and you see what the ghoul looks like, his nose falls off, parts of the body just start to literally disintegrate. That’s based on radiation exposure. That’s essentially what happened to these women.

Oh! It is like an implantable radiation pellet, the kind we actually still use to treat certain cancers, except it’s in your jaw, irradiating you constantly from the inside.

Yes. And the cruelest part is that the factory managers knew. They knew these women weren’t just getting sick with some mysterious female illness. They were being poisoned, and they kept going anyway. Eventually, a scrappy pro bono attorney took up their case, and they won, though the lead plaintiff died before seeing the outcome. The monetary damages were almost beside the point. The real consequence was OSHA, the entire framework of workplace safety regulation. The reason you can’t knowingly expose employees to toxic substances, the reason we have chemical documentation requirements in workplaces, all of that started with these young women and their rotting teeth and bones.

Radium has a half-life of 1200 years. It wasn’t until we started putting it in paint and putting those paintbrushes in the mouths of young women that we got real problems. There was a specific vulnerability. It has an affinity for teeth and the jawbone.

Yes, teeth are literally the worst place for it. And teenage brains are the worst place for a dopamine-hit algorithm. They don’t have the same brakes that adults do. The developing brain is particularly susceptible to sex, drugs, and rock and roll. That’s all dopamine. And that’s what these algorithms are doing, to the point that teenagers aren’t even that interested in sex, drugs, and rock and roll anymore. They’re interested in their TikTok feed, because it’s so much more immediately exciting. It’s like a biosimilar. Instead of doing the things teenagers were supposed to do, instead of calcium in your teeth, they have this instead. It doesn’t belong in their brains in this way, and yet there it is.

So who are our modern Radium Girls?

I believe they are the young adolescent girls, and it’s not only girls, but the lawsuits happen to involve girls, who have become completely immersed in social media algorithms to the point where cutting, eating disorders, and suicidality are literally woven into the fiber of their beings. The algorithms have hijacked their dopamine reward systems, and they can’t extricate themselves. Just like radium was incorporated into bone, this is incorporated into how their brains work. It’s not a toxic chemical. It’s a toxic technology.

What did these two verdicts reveal about what these companies knew?

The New Mexico case centers on encrypted chat. Meta essentially claimed they didn’t know child predators were using the platform to communicate with minors, but of course they did. The same targeting technology that shows you shoes after you’ve been searching for them works just as well for predators seeking children.

They were advertising encrypted chat products to sexual predators.

That is the case, or at a minimum, they simply chose not to put in safeguards. Woeful negligence, the same as when the factory managers realized the women were being poisoned by the paint and kept going anyway.

The trial record bears this out. Meta maintained a 17-strike policy for accounts engaged in sex trafficking, meaning a user could accumulate 16 violations before removal. Instagram’s former head of safety testified that by any measure across the industry, it was “a very, very high strike threshold.” A separate 2021 internal Meta presentation estimated that 100,000 children per day received online sexual harassment via its platforms. Internal documents referenced in the case show Meta stalled efforts to address predator access to minors due to “growth concerns.”

The California verdict uses a product defect theory, arguing the product itself is flawed, the way a car with faulty brakes is defective. A young woman was being served self-harm content repeatedly, and the argument was that the product fostered that. That verdict came in around $6 million, which is literally seconds of Meta’s annual revenue.

Personally, I think the New Mexico case is more significant because the product is not defective. Anyone who thinks it’s defective doesn’t understand how tech companies work. The product is doing exactly what it was designed to do. It’s dangerous by design. They want maximum engagement, and if the content driving that engagement happens to be self-harm content, well, that’s the algorithm working as intended. That’s not a defect. It’s a feature they chose not to restrain.

These were jury verdicts, actual evidence presented to real people who reached a conclusion. And historically, these companies hid behind Section 230. Everyone was just “talking on the phone” except on their platform. What these lawsuits acknowledge is that an algorithm exists. It’s not just a phone line. It’s a product that actively feeds you something, and that’s what caused the harm.

That argument simply does not hold up anymore. If you have a message board and some random person posts something weird, you can see how liability would be challenging. But if your product is not a passive message board but is actively curating and selecting content, including dangerous content, that is a fundamentally different matter. And that’s what these platforms do. That’s why they’re free. You are the product. They’re selling your attention to the companies that actually pay.

Meta’s own researchers knew what they had. When their internal Project Mercury study found that people who stopped using Facebook for a week reported lower feelings of depression, anxiety, loneliness, and social comparison, the company shut the project down and declared the results were tainted by “the existing media narrative.” One Meta employee warned colleagues that if the findings leaked, it was going to look like tobacco companies doing research and knowing cigarettes were bad and then keeping that information to themselves. They made the comparison themselves.

And it’s more valuable to advertisers the longer you stay on. So when you build your model around advertising, you simultaneously build your model around capturing every possible moment of a child’s life on that platform.

Yes. It would be like using cocaine to lure people to watch advertisements. Not just free cocaine, free cocaine that keeps refilling itself, sends you push notifications when your friends are using, and never asks whether you’d like to stop. That’s infinite scroll. It’s not just an open-air drug market. It’s a dealer who says, “I see your cocaine is running low, here’s more. You didn’t ask, I’m just giving it to you. You can stop whenever you want, but I’m going to keep going until you tell me to stop.” By the way, your friends are over here taking a bump right now, so you might be missing out.

In an internal chat entered into evidence, Meta researchers described their own product thusly: “IG is a drug… we’re basically pushers.”

An open-air drug market for children.

And the product is completely free, which removes one of the few natural checks on overconsumption. As long as these things are free with no consequence, I don’t see how this gets solved, even with age-gating.

You’ve suggested pricing might be part of the solution?

Part of what drove down cigarette use wasn’t just age restrictions; it was taxes that made them genuinely expensive. I think there’s a completely viable business model where people pay for social media use, say, a free hour a day, and a charge after that. Parents who can’t spend unlimited money would have a built-in check. Kids understand finite resources. They know we can’t buy infinite Robux. Right now, there’s nothing to stop someone from being on Instagram forever, and every incentive for the platform to make sure they are.

And AI is facing some of the same questions. It’s like they took medical-grade AI and made it non-prescription and free. Our own daughter, Quinn, pointed this out.

Well, keep putting that radium in your mouth, keep on scrolling. Compute isn’t free, and the companies that have chosen not to rely on advertising seem to be doing just fine. Anthropic has decided to charge for use rather than run ads, and they’re viable. You can’t have it both ways and maintain your integrity. Nothing truly valuable should be free in this way. Attention is a finite resource. We need to do other things with our lives.

So, where does this go from here?

These verdicts, even though the dollar amounts are small, signal a shift in perception. The liability is becoming real. And what I hope follows, what has to follow, the way OSHA followed the Radium Girls, is actual regulation. Not just fines that get treated as a cost of doing business, but enforceable product standards. Infinite scroll should simply not be allowed. The pillow I’m looking at right now has more regulation applied to it than these platforms do. The App Store already makes medical apps jump through extensive hoops. It could decide it won’t carry products with certain features. Government consumer protection agencies need to set actual standards.

Once you know your product is harming people and you keep going anyway, you have liability. And the fines have to be existential, the kind that would actually change behavior, not the kind that big players just absorb while smaller competitors get pushed out. That’s what happened with big tobacco, and they’re still here.

In 2021, when asked whether child safety was his top concern, Zuckerberg replied that he had “a number of other areas I’m more focused on, like building the metaverse.”

It’s a compelling comparison. The Radium Girls gave us OSHA. What do you think the social media plaintiffs might give us?

I think they’ll give us the regulatory framework we should have built at the start. We’re in the same moment that manufacturing was in during the 1910s and 1920s; society is transforming around a new technology faster than the rules can keep up. And just like then, it’s going to take the visible suffering of vulnerable young women, working hard, wanting to be something, being preyed upon, before we finally say this is not okay. We regulate everything else. We can regulate this.

Radium is still with us. It treats bone cancer. It has real value. Social media is not all bad, either. We just decided that some ways of using radium were unacceptable. That’s all anyone is asking here.

Carlene MacMillan, MD, FCTMSS, DFAACAP, is a psychiatrist, Chief Product Officer at Radial, and co-chair of the Public Resource Committee at the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. She is also the mother of our children, Trent and Quinn.
